brief.head: Opiate of the asses
brief.text: Conspiracy the­o­ries, Ajay Shah said, are “the opi­ate of the asses”: the world is so com­pli­cated that to be­lieve one, you have to be sim­ple-minded. {006-J03}

brief.head: Slogans beat stories
brief.text: Populists win on sim­plis­tic nar­ra­tives, Amit Varma ar­gued. Trump’s 2016 story of lost jobs, “China bad”, was ap­peal­ing but false; the com­plex truth makes no slo­gan. {006-C04}

brief.head: Safety before plenty
brief.text: Safety and free­dom come be­fore pros­per­ity, Ajay Shah ar­gued, so Deng Xiaoping’s record is open to ques­tion. Amit Varma replied that es­cap­ing poverty is an ab­so­lute value. {006-C10}

brief.head: Two candlesticks
brief.text: Amit Varma was the first per­son to win the Bastiat Prize twice. Its tro­phy, a can­dle­stick, nods to the can­dle­mak­ers who pe­ti­tioned to block out the sun. {006-S02}

brief.head: A 19th-century man
brief.text: Ajay Shah counts him­self part of economics’ 19th-century tra­di­tion, closer to the dreams of Ricardo, Adam Smith and Marx. Today’s eco­nom­ics, he said, is “a pale shadow”. {006-J19}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on Bastiat and Hayek
lead.head: Two Freddies and a broken window

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 6

body: Amit Varma named his friend Freddie after two he­roes: the 19th-century French writer Frédéric Bastiat and the econ­o­mist Friedrich Hayek. In this episode he and Ajay Shah told Freddie’s deep, dark back­story.

Between them, the two Freddies offer a way of see­ing the world. Bastiat taught that every pol­icy has ef­fects you can see and ef­fects you can­not. Hayek showed why no plan­ner can know enough to run an econ­omy, and why prices do the job in­stead.

Bastiat’s para­ble of the bro­ken win­dow sets the pat­tern. People say a bro­ken win­dow is good for the econ­omy, be­cause the glazier gets paid. {#window} What is not seen, Varma said, is what the owner would have done with that money: bought a coat, per­haps, or a cake.
A bad econ­o­mist, he said, looks only at first-order ef­fects. A good one takes ev­ery­thing into ac­count.
## From the poor to the rich

From that habit of mind, Varma drew his cen­tral claim. “Most gov­ern­ment in­ter­ven­tions in the econ­omy, in the mar­ket, if not all, re­dis­tribute wealth from the poor to the rich,” he said. He wanted it in cap­i­tal let­ters. {006-C05}

Tariffs are a great ex­am­ple, he said. Shield a local teddy-bear maker from a cheaper Chinese rival, and each buyer pays ten ru­pees more. Each barely no­tices the loss; the local lobby col­lects the lot.

Shah added a darker twist. Blowing up a rail­road or a port would raise costs once and for all. A tar­iff can be granted or with­drawn, in­dus­try by in­dus­try, giv­ing the state “Godlike power over the en­tre­pre­neur­ial class”. {006-C06}
Bastiat called it plun­der when peo­ple seize what oth­ers pro­duce. When hon­est profit is too hard, Varma said, peo­ple seek rent in­stead.
## Makers and tak­ers

Shah took the ar­gu­ment to China. There, he said, party-connected tak­ers have re­peat­edly used state power against mak­ers, until en­trepreneurs learned to put party mem­bers on their boards and princelings among their share­hold­ers.
“A gov­ern­ment that will give you any­thing that you want is a gov­ern­ment that can take away ev­ery­thing that you have,” he said.
Shah also of­fered a hope­ful coun­ter­point. Jeff Bezos’s *Washington Post* went after Donald Trump, and the President could nei­ther shut it down nor hit back at Bezos. {006-S08}
## Prices as mes­sen­gers

Hayek’s essay *The Use of Knowledge in Society* an­swered calls for a cen­tral com­mit­tee to set every price. The knowl­edge an econ­omy runs on, Shah ex­plained, is scat­tered across ev­ery­one: one person’s need for a taxi, another’s will­ing­ness to drive. No plan­ner can gather it all.

Prices co­or­di­nate ev­ery­one with­out any­one need­ing to talk. Varma keeps re­turn­ing to Uber’s surge pric­ing, which lets those who value a ride most pay for it and calls an idle driver out from his lunch.
Cap the price and the scarcity stays; only the sup­ply van­ishes. “People sim­ply don’t re­alise that you can­not leg­is­late scarcity away,” Varma said. {006-C14}
The hosts ended with books. Shah chose Milton Friedman’s *Capitalism and Freedom*, whose chap­ters each struck him “like an earth­quake”; Varma, Henry Hazlitt’s *Economics in One Lesson*.

Capitalism, Varma said, equals con­sent: many peo­ple act­ing vol­un­tar­ily in dou­ble thank-you mo­ments, where buyer and seller both come out ahead. It is often con­fused with crony­ism, he added, which is its op­po­site.

second.label: Frédéric Bastiat
second.head: All the breath he had
second.deck: Amit Varma on the French economist who died at 49, his own age

pic.caption: Frédéric Bastiat in an 1848 lithograph
pic.credit: Émile Desmaisons. Lithograph by Auguste-Hilaire Léveillé., public domain

body: Frédéric Bastiat, the 19th-century French writer, econ­o­mist and par­lia­men­tar­ian, died at 49. That, Amit Varma noted sadly, is his own age. {#fortynine}

Bastiat caught tu­ber­cu­lo­sis while trav­el­ling around France to pop­u­larise his ideas. Knowing his lungs were fail­ing, and re­fer­ring, Varma thinks, to his book *The Law*, he vowed to pro­claim his prin­ci­ple until the day of his death. {006-S01}

The econ­o­mist Joseph Schumpeter called him the most bril­liant eco­nomic jour­nal­ist who ever lived. {006-J13} Varma said Bastiat ex­plained ideas like op­por­tu­nity cost be­fore such terms were in much use, and won­dered what he could have done with many more years. Ajay Shah’s con­so­la­tion: Varma has fifty more years, and owes the world “five big books”.

quote.text: I shall pro­claim this prin­ci­ple with all the force of my lungs, which alas is all too in­ad­e­quate.

third.head: Jeeps, judges and Indira

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Indira Gandhi and the government jeeps

body: Raj Narain, Ajay Shah re­called, dragged Indira Gandhi to Justice Sinha’s court­room in the Allahabad High Court over a “sweet lit­tle prob­lem”: using some gov­ern­ment jeeps for cam­paign­ing. {006-S06}

The point, Shah said, was the sep­a­ra­tion. There is the Congress party and there is the gov­ern­ment, and the gov­ern­ment owns the jeeps. Use them to cam­paign and your elec­tion is in­val­i­dated. That, he said, was India in 1975.
“We in India should be very, very proud,” he said. “Don’t you love it?”

China has never had such con­sti­tu­tional niceties, Shah ar­gued. There the party is the state and the state is the party. {#partystate} Its busi­nesses learned, in time, to serve at the plea­sure of the party.

p2.title: Unseen and unplanned
p2.deck: Frédéric Bastiat on the unseen, Friedrich Hayek on the price system, as argued over by Amit Varma and Ajay Shah

from1.head: Two Freddies and a broken window

quote.text: A bad econ­o­mist will only look at your first order ef­fect. But a good econ­o­mist will take ev­ery­thing into ac­count

box.title: The essay behind the podcast
box.text: Amit Varma’s pod­cast, *The Seen and the Unseen*, is in­spired by Bastiat’s essay *That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen*. It be­gins with the para­ble of the bro­ken win­dow and asks you to look past a policy’s vis­i­ble ef­fect. {006-R01}

sections.label: Bastiat’s lens
sections.head: The coat nobody bought
sections.caption: the seen and the unseen
body: Frédéric Bastiat’s essay *That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen* opens with a bro­ken win­dow. Onlookers say it is good for the econ­omy, be­cause the man who re­pairs it gets paid. {#window}
That is what is seen, Amit Varma said. What is not seen is what the owner would have done with the money had it been left with him: bought a coat, say, or a cake.

The same fal­lacy, he said, lies be­hind the ar­gu­ment that war is good for the econ­omy. {#war} Such con­se­quences are often un­in­tended, but not un­fore­seen: once you un­der­stand eco­nomic laws, you can fore­see many of them.
## Ditches and sur­prises

Varma ap­plies the lens to GDP. He ob­jects to count­ing gov­ern­ment spend­ing in it, an ar­gu­ment he said Keynes and oth­ers won be­fore the Second World War. A gov­ern­ment could tax peo­ple to dig ditches and fill them, and GDP would keep grow­ing. “And every met­ric can be gamed,” he said. {006-C02}
Ajay Shah traced the idea to the so­ci­ol­o­gist Robert K. Merton, in 1936, he seemed to think: all pur­po­sive so­cial ac­tion has un­in­tended con­se­quences. {#merton}
Beyond the ob­vi­ous ef­fects, Shah said, the world will sur­prise us: “we only dimly un­der­stand the full con­se­quences of all-purposive so­cial ac­tion.” {006-C03}
~ Varma’s first plan for his own pod­cast, *The Seen and the Unseen*, was short episodes on pub­lic poli­cies, bust­ing one fal­lacy at a time.

quote.text: A bad econ­o­mist will only look at your first order ef­fect. But a good econ­o­mist will take ev­ery­thing into ac­count

art.caption: Amit Varma on the seen and the unseen

sections.label: Poor to rich
sections.head: Robin Hood runs backwards
sections.caption: tariffs and the teddy bear
body: Frédéric Bastiat’s ge­nius, Amit Varma said, was to dis­til com­plex ideas into sto­ries ev­ery­body could un­der­stand. In *The Candlemakers’ Petition*, the can­dle­mak­ers ask who­ever ruled France to block out the sun. {#candles}

Another satire seeks a ban on work­ing with the right hand, since more ef­fort was sup­posed to mean more pros­per­ity. A third an­swers for­eign com­pe­ti­tion by de­stroy­ing the rail­roads. {#railroads}

Varma’s mod­ern ver­sion in­volves teddy bears. A local maker sells at 100 ru­pees; a Chinese rival sells at 90. The gov­ern­ment puts a 20-rupee tar­iff on the im­port, which now costs 110. {#tariff}
Ten ru­pees moves from each buyer to the local maker, who also loses the in­cen­tive to raise his game. Public choice the­ory calls this dif­fuse costs and con­cen­trated ben­e­fits. {#diffuse}
## A sword over busi­ness
Ajay Shah asked why a state would choose tar­iffs over blow­ing up a rail­road or the JNPT, India’s big­gest con­tainer port, when the ef­fect on prices is the same. {#jnpt}

Blowing up the port is a one-time de­ci­sion, he said. A tar­iff can be granted, re­moved or brought back, in­dus­try by in­dus­try, leav­ing cap­i­tal­ists dan­gling. That beats a sim­ple trans­fer from the poor to the rich.
~ Follow the in­cen­tives, Varma added, and party po­si­tions make sense. The AAP op­poses FDI in re­tail, and many of its big­gest sup­port­ers are small re­tail­ers.

quote.text: So the cost is dif­fused among a large va­ri­ety of peo­ple. I lose 10 ru­pees, I won’t even no­tice.

art.caption: Amit Varma on tariffs and the teddy bear

sections.label: Two ways to get rich
sections.head: Plunder by permit
sections.caption: makers, takers and refuge
body: In *The Law*, Frédéric Bastiat named two ways to live: by ap­ply­ing your own fac­ul­ties, the ori­gin of prop­erty, or by seiz­ing what oth­ers pro­duce, the ori­gin of plun­der. Today, Amit Varma said, plun­der mostly runs through the co­er­cive power of the state, as rent-seeking and crony­ism.

Jagdish Bhagwati once said, Varma re­called, that the Chinese were turn­ing out to be profit-seeking and Indians rent-seeking. Varma does not know enough about China to judge, but for India it rings true.

People choose which­ever path is less bur­den­some, Bastiat ar­gued. “If it is eas­ier to seek profit, you will seek profit,” Varma said. {006-C07} In India’s first decades hon­est trade was too hard, and a rent-seeking men­tal­ity took hold.
## The price of refuge

Ajay Shah’s terms were mak­ers and tak­ers. Makers build prod­ucts and or­gan­i­sa­tions that serve con­sumers. Takers grab, and once the state holds a mo­nop­oly on vi­o­lence, they grab through reg­u­la­tions and rules.
Protection from the state, Shah said, al­ways costs some­thing, in un­pre­dictable de­mands that come later. {006-C08}

~ Bastiat’s dystopia, Varma replied, is the mod­ern world, where the state is all-powerful and the mak­ers fight against the odds. Bastiat would have recog­nised India and China, he said, and Russia with some hor­ror.

quote.text: Every form of refuge has a price.

art.caption: Amit Varma on makers, takers and refuge

sections.label: Hayek’s prices
sections.head: The fare that finds a driver
sections.caption: surge pricing and price caps
body: Friedrich Hayek’s *The Use of Knowledge in Society*, which Amit Varma called the most im­por­tant and sem­i­nal essay of the twen­ti­eth cen­tury, ar­gued against Oscar Lange’s pro­posal for a cen­tral price com­mit­tee. {006-J15}
Frédéric Bastiat had made a sim­i­lar point about Paris, Varma said. No com­mit­tee de­cides who eats what, yet the city, al­most mirac­u­lously and with­out co­or­di­na­tion, feeds it­self.

Varma’s ev­ery­day ex­am­ple is Uber. If 200 peo­ple want cabs and only 20 are avail­able, a price cap hands them to the first 20, even some­one ca­su­ally off to the mall while an­other needs a hos­pi­tal. {#taxis}
Surge pric­ing lets those who value a ride most pay for it. More im­por­tant, Varma said, it sig­nals an idle driver to come out and make money by serv­ing oth­ers. {006-C13}
## No law against scarcity
Price con­trols al­ways lead to short­ages, he said. Decree that a car should cost no more than ten thou­sand, and ex­ist­ing cars are snapped up and pro­duc­tion stops. {#cars}

About three years be­fore the record­ing, Delhi’s AAP gov­ern­ment had just ex­per­i­mented with a price cap on Uber when a friend of Varma’s could not get a cab to the air­port and missed his flight. {006-S04}
~ When the gov­ern­ment capped the price of stents, Varma pre­dicted short­ages and deaths. “Exactly that hap­pened,” he said.

quote.text: The price car­ried in­for­ma­tion, the price car­ried an in­cen­tive, and more and more cabs get on the street be­cause they want to make money

sections.label: Order without design
sections.head: No one ordered this pencil
sections.caption: discovery, not design
body: Many beau­ti­ful things, Amit Varma said, are what Adam Ferguson called “the prod­uct of human ac­tion but not human de­sign”: the way cities and economies func­tion, the way lan­guages evolve, even nat­u­ral se­lec­tion. {006-J16}
Ajay Shah prefers a phrase from math­e­mat­ics and sci­ence, the self-organising sys­tem: local de­ci­sions, no cen­tral con­trol, re­mark­able re­sults.

Friedrich Hayek’s in­sight, Shah said, has two parts. The knowl­edge of pref­er­ences and cir­cum­stances is dis­persed across so­ci­ety, so “a plan­ner will al­ways get it wrong”. And prices co­or­di­nate us, so no­body need agree who plays Hamlet and who plays Ophelia. {006-C12}
## The con­ceit re­turns

If the twen­ti­eth cen­tury taught one bumper-sticker les­son, Shah said, it is that cen­tral plan­ning brings stag­na­tion. Yet the com­puter rev­o­lu­tion keeps re­viv­ing the planner’s dream, a game of whack-a-mole. “We should let the world be a process of dis­cov­ery, not de­sign,” he said. {006-C11}

Varma re­called Adam Smith’s “man of sys­tem”, who imag­ines he can treat the world like a board of chess. Leonard Read’s essay *I, Pencil* shows the op­po­site: a pencil’s parts come from some forty or fifty coun­tries, from peo­ple who never talk to one an­other. {#pencil}
~ For Shah, a card-carrying econ­o­mist, the price sys­tem is the heart and soul of eco­nom­ics. He would have COVID vac­cines traded on free mar­kets, with fu­tures con­tracts.

quote.text: We are all AGIs that are walk­ing this planet try­ing to do things for our­selves.

art.caption: Amit Varma on discovery, not design

quote.text: I keep telling peo­ple that what is cap­i­tal­ism? It’s the vol­un­tary ac­tions of many peo­ple com­ing to­gether. You’re play­ing pos­i­tive sum games. It’s dou­ble thank you mo­ments.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: From a Chinese boardroom to a Gujarat village, and what each one teaches

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on China’s makers, takers and princelings
stories.head: The princeling on the board
body: In Ajay Shah’s telling, China’s en­trepreneurs met their state in stages. At first there was some gen­uine prom­ise. {#phaseone} You could have an idea, find cool tech­nol­ogy, serve the con­sumer, build a com­plex or­gan­i­sa­tion and make money, fair and square.
But in China there is not much of a line be­tween the state and the Chinese Communist Party. “The party is the state and the state is the party,” Shah said.

Then, again and again, tak­ers used state power against mak­ers. A maker would be driven into dis­tress and sell a per­fectly nice busi­ness for a song, or be forced to shut down while the taker grabbed the mar­ket.

Capitalists got the point. In what Shah thinks of as the last 15 years, any sig­nif­i­cant busi­ness has needed party mem­bers on its board, or princelings, the chil­dren of party lead­ers, as share­hold­ers. {#fifteen}

He voiced the prag­matic en­tre­pre­neur. “Chodo yaar, I have to get three party peo­ple as my board mem­bers. I’ll do it.” Twenty per cent of the shares to a princeling? No prob­lem: he keeps his 80 per cent, and the fix­ing has been done. {#princeling}

Such pro­tec­tion is never free, Shah said: a state that can give you any­thing can take ev­ery­thing away. {006-S07} Demands fol­low at un­pre­dictable dates, from “give this guy a job” to chang­ing how a prod­uct is run. It amounts to tax­a­tion not cod­i­fied in law, as be­fore the Magna Carta, and China has had an in­vest­ment slump.
~ Russia, he said, is a step fur­ther. There Putin de­cides whether an oli­garch goes to jail, is sent into exile or is mur­dered in London.
stories.why: Wealth means lit­tle un­less it can stand up to the state. Entrepreneurs who ac­cept the fix­ing, Shah ar­gued, are not think­ing two moves ahead; to be in busi­ness, he said, you need to be a philoso­pher.
stories.postscript: Shah’s hope­ful coun­terex­am­ple: Jeff Bezos’s *Washington Post* went after Donald Trump, and the fed­eral gov­ern­ment could not hit back. {006-S08}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on China’s makers and takers

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on bread prices after a Gujarat earthquake
stories.head: Dear bread, shared bread
body: Around 1993 or 1994, Amit Varma, then a stu­dent, vol­un­teered after an earth­quake in Gujarat and rode in an am­bu­lance with a bunch of paramedics. {006-S03}
They stopped at a vil­lage where all the build­ings had col­lapsed. A cou­ple of shops were open, and they had raised the price of bread three or four times. {#bread}

His in­stant thought, Varma said, was: “Oh man, this is evil. This is just freak­ing evil.” Later he saw it as the price sys­tem at play. Instead of the first fam­ily buy­ing up all the bread, two fam­i­lies could pool their money, so ev­ery­body got a cou­ple of slices.
~ “Things are what they are,” he said, “and price con­trols al­ways lead to short­ages.”
stories.why: In a cri­sis, moral in­stinct and eco­nomic logic can point op­po­site ways. A high price ra­tions a scarce good so it gets shared; a capped one lets the first comer take ev­ery­thing. {006-C14}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on bread after the earthquake

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s question, and Ajay Shah’s answer
stories.head: We didn’t start the fire, Ken did
body: Amit Varma some­times asks peo­ple who has had the great­est pos­i­tive im­pact on hu­man­ity in the last 30 years. His own top can­di­date was Jeff Bezos, until a friend made the case for Deng Xiaoping, who lifted hun­dreds of mil­lions of Chinese out of poverty.
Ajay Shah’s ver­dict on Deng bor­rowed from Zhou Enlai: “It’s too soon to tell.” {006-J06}
His own pick was Ken Thompson, the main in­ven­tor of Unix. “And we didn’t start the fire, Ken did.” {006-J07}

~ On Deng, Shah said that the intra-party demo­cratic in­sti­tu­tions and term lim­its he man­aged to cre­ate have peeled away. Varma held his ground: lift­ing hun­dreds of mil­lions of peo­ple out of poverty, he said, was a stag­ger­ing achieve­ment.
stories.why: Each an­swer shows what its giver val­ues most. Shah of­fered a re­lated ex­er­cise: go back in a time ma­chine to 1978 and ask what you would tell Deng, or Nehru. {#timemachine}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the greatest human of the last 30 years

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on an economist who sneered at Hazlitt’s readers
stories.head: One lesson is plenty
body: A cou­ple of years ago, Amit Varma re­called, an econ­o­mist both hosts know made a snarky com­ment: too many peo­ple ar­gu­ing with him had only read Henry Hazlitt’s *Economics in One Lesson*. {006-S10}
This was an econ­o­mist who, not sur­pris­ingly in Varma’s view, had de­fended de­mon­eti­sa­tion, or at least ar­gued for a wait-and-watch ap­proach.

Varma’s re­sponse: “That’s enough. Those peo­ple know more than you, right? They know the first prin­ci­ples.” You have to start there, he said, and “a physi­cist who does not be­lieve in grav­ity is not a physi­cist I would trust.” {006-J11}

~ Hazlitt’s book uses basic prin­ci­ples to ex­plain price con­trols, tar­iffs and in­fla­tion. It has sold more than a mil­lion copies and is avail­able in some 40 to 50 lan­guages, Varma said. {#hazlitt}

quote.text: Economics is not a sub­ject that should be left to the econ­o­mists.

quiz.q: Why did a friend of Amit Varma’s miss a flight from Delhi?
quiz.a: Delhi’s gov­ern­ment had just capped Uber prices, and he could not get a cab.

quiz.q: Whose central price committee was Hayek’s *The Use of Knowledge in Society* written against?
quiz.a: The econ­o­mist Oscar Lange’s, who wanted a com­mit­tee to de­cide every price.

glossary.def: Getting rich by using state power to take, not make.
Order that arises from human ac­tion, not human de­sign.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 6. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Friedrich Hayek (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0); Frédéric Bastiat (Émile Desmaisons. Lithograph by Auguste-Hilaire Léveillé., public domain); Adam Smith (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Milton Friedman (Bachrach Studios, public domain).

shelf.title: That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen
shelf.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
shelf.why: Bastiat’s bro­ken-window para­ble, which teaches you to look past a policy’s vis­i­ble ef­fect to its un­seen costs and in­tro­duced op­por­tu­nity cost decades be­fore the term ex­isted.

shelf.title: The Law
shelf.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
shelf.why: Bastiat’s mid-19th-century mas­ter­piece on the re­la­tion­ship be­tween the state and so­ci­ety, which Amit says car­ries wis­dom in every para­graph and is a strik­ingly mod­ern lens on India.

shelf.title: Economic Sophisms
shelf.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
shelf.why: Bastiat could boil com­plex ideas down to sto­ries any­one un­der­stands, show­ing how ab­surd pro­tec­tion­ism and the ‘more work equals more prosperity’ fal­lacy are.

shelf.title: The Candlemakers’ Petition
shelf.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
shelf.why: Bastiat’s satire takes pro­tec­tion­ist logic se­ri­ously until it reaches ab­sur­dity; once you’ve laughed at it, you can’t take ‘save local businesses’ rhetoric at face value.

shelf.title: The Use of Knowledge in Society
shelf.creator: Friedrich Hayek
shelf.why: Hayek’s ar­gu­ment that the knowl­edge needed to run an econ­omy is dis­persed among mil­lions of peo­ple, and that prices, not plan­ners, carry it: a lan­guage through which strangers tell each other what they want and lack.

shelf.title: The Fatal Conceit
shelf.creator: Friedrich Hayek
shelf.why: Hayek names the core error be­hind cen­tral plan­ning and price con­trols: the be­lief that any­one can know enough to run a com­plex so­ci­ety from the top down, when the knowl­edge it needs is spread across ev­ery­one.

shelf.title: A primer on Hayek
shelf.creator: Eamonn Butler
shelf.why: Butler’s short primer on Hayek, a friendly way into a thinker whose own books can be heavy going (‘though what a great writer’, Amit adds).

shelf.title: I, Pencil
shelf.creator: Leonard Read
shelf.why: A pen­cil nar­rates its own mak­ing from ma­te­ri­als and know-how scat­tered across many coun­tries, co­or­di­nated by prices with no one in charge.

shelf.title: I, Pencil (The Movie)
shelf.why: A filmed ver­sion of the pen­cil para­ble for those who pre­fer watch­ing to read­ing.

shelf.title: The Evolution of Everything
shelf.creator: Matt Ridley
shelf.why: Ridley finds the same bot­tom-up process, with no plan­ner or de­signer, be­hind nat­u­ral se­lec­tion, lan­guage, prices, cul­tural norms and com­mon law.

shelf.title: The Evolution of Everything (Episode 96 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Matt Ridley
shelf.why: Amit’s long con­ver­sa­tion with Matt Ridley, a com­pan­ion to his book, on how order emerges bot­tom-up with­out cen­tral de­sign, across bi­ol­ogy, cul­ture and mar­kets.

shelf.title: The Blind Watchmaker
shelf.creator: Richard Dawkins
shelf.why: Dawkins shows how in­tri­cate de­sign, like the eye, arises with­out a de­signer: the bi­o­log­i­cal coun­ter­part of Hayek’s point about economies.

shelf.title: Demystifying GDP (Episode 130 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Rajeswari Sengupta
shelf.why: Rajeswari Sengupta on what GDP can and can­not mea­sure and how the num­ber is built, in­clud­ing how gov­ern­ment make-work and roads to nowhere in­flate it.

shelf.title: The Great Redistribution
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s ar­gu­ment that mar­ket in­ter­ven­tions such as tar­iffs or bans on FDI in re­tail qui­etly move money from many dis­persed, poor con­sumers to a few or­gan­ised, rich in­ter­est groups, the op­po­site of their stated in­ten­tion.

shelf.title: Price Controls Lead to Shortages and Harm the Poor
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s case that you can­not leg­is­late scarcity away: price caps dis­cour­age pro­duc­ers and in­no­va­tors, so goods don’t get cheaper but van­ish into short­ages and black mar­kets, hurt­ing the poor they claim to pro­tect.

shelf.title: What is Populism?
shelf.creator: Jan-Werner Müller
shelf.why: The book that taught Amit most of what he knows about pop­ulism: it re­places the naive ‘pop­ulism = popular’ with a pre­cise check­list for spot­ting pop­ulists any­where.

shelf.title: Why Both Modi and Trump are Textbook Populists
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit ap­plies Müller’s frame­work to two con­tem­po­rary lead­ers and shows how slo­gan-sized sto­ries crowd out com­plex truths.

shelf.title: Crowds and Power
shelf.creator: Elias Canetti
shelf.why: Useful for un­der­stand­ing how anger gets mo­bilised into an ‘us vs them’ route to power.

shelf.title: The Double ‘Thank You’ Moment
shelf.creator: John Stossel
shelf.why: Stossel’s sim­plest pic­ture of pos­i­tive-sum ex­change: when you buy a cof­fee, you thank the barista and the barista thanks you, be­cause both are bet­ter off.

shelf.title: Capitalism and Freedom
shelf.creator: Milton Friedman
shelf.why: Not an in­tro­duc­tory book, but Ajay says each chap­ter is ‘like an earthquake’ that shakes you into think­ing about the world; part of the foun­da­tional read­ing be­hind Amit’s un­der­stand­ing of mar­kets and free­dom.

shelf.title: Free to Choose
shelf.creator: Milton and Rose Friedman
shelf.why: The Friedmans’ case for vol­un­tary ex­change, which Amit uses to argue that cap­i­tal­ism means con­sent and is the op­po­site of crony­ism; a core text on his ‘rec­om­mend ev­ery­thing by Friedman’ list.

shelf.title: Economics in One Lesson
shelf.creator: Henry Hazlitt
shelf.why: Hazlitt’s 1946 ‘col­lec­tion of light bulbs’ that uses the ba­sics of scarcity and in­cen­tives to clear up fal­la­cies about price con­trols, tar­iffs, in­fla­tion and gov­ern­ment spend­ing, teach­ing you to ask what the money would have done if left with con­sumers.

shelf.title: Fear the Boom and Bust: Keynes vs. Hayek (economics rap battle)
shelf.why: A rap bat­tle be­tween ac­tors play­ing Keynes and Hayek, with lyrics by EconTalk’s Russ Roberts, which the hosts rec­om­mend to­gether with its se­quel, Fight of the Century: a de­light­ful way into the clash be­tween the two dom­i­nant eco­nomic schools of the 20th cen­tury.

shelf.title: Fight of the Century: Keynes vs. Hayek (Economics Rap Battle Round Two)
shelf.why: Round two of the same play­ful take on the great de­bate.

laughs.text: Producer Vartika’s T-shirt line about Karjat, where the episode was recorded: ‘Badi Badi Baatein, Wada Pao Khaate’ (big talk while eat­ing vada pav). Amit says it seems tar­geted at the two of them, and Ajay says Karjat has the best vada pav in the world.

The episode is framed around Amit’s ‘friend Freddie’, who must be kept in the frame and is named after his two he­roes, Frédéric Bastiat and Friedrich Hayek. During his teddy-bear tar­iff ex­am­ple Amit adds, ‘No one is bet­ter than my Freddy.’ At the end he sug­gests Milton Friedman could be a Freddy too ‘if you twist his sur­name around a bit.’
Ajay on con­spir­acy the­o­ries: ‘con­spir­acy the­o­ries are the opi­ate of the asses’, be­cause to be­lieve one ‘you have to be sim­ple-minded.’

Bastiat’s satires as Amit retells them: can­dle­mak­ers pe­ti­tion­ing to block out the sun, a pe­ti­tion to ban ev­ery­one from work­ing with their right hand (since more ef­fort sup­pos­edly means more pros­per­ity), and the ‘neg­a­tive railroad’ so­lu­tion to for­eign com­pe­ti­tion: de­stroy the rail­roads.
Amit on GDP: with gov­ern­ment spend­ing counted, you can keep ‘dig­ging up ditches, fill­ing them, dig­ging up ditches, fill­ing them, and the GDP is just grow­ing and grow­ing.’
Asked about Deng Xiaoping’s legacy, Ajay quotes Zhou Enlai: ‘it’s too soon to tell.’
Ajay names Ken Thompson, main in­ven­tor of Unix, as the great­est human of the last 30 years, riff­ing on the song line: ‘we didn’t start the fire, Ken did.’
Ajay, after Amit says Bastiat died at 49, Amit’s own age: ‘you have fifty more years to go... you owe the world five big books in your next fifty years.’

Ajay voices a prag­matic Chinese en­tre­pre­neur cut­ting deals with the party: ‘Chodo yaar, I have to get three party peo­ple as my board mem­bers. I’ll do it... Anyway, I keep my 80%, no?’ The fix­ing has been done. Meanwhile, a Russian bil­lion­aire who owns a crit­i­cal news­pa­per ‘will just ex­pe­ri­ence some ac­ci­dents, you’ll fall out of a win­dow.’

Amit on arm­chair econ­o­mists: ev­ery­body gives gyan on eco­nom­ics, though no­body would give gyan on nu­clear physics with­out study­ing it. And ‘a physi­cist who does not be­lieve in grav­ity is not a physi­cist I would trust.’
Joseph Schumpeter called Bastiat ‘the most bril­liant eco­nomic jour­nal­ist who ever lived’.
Jagdish Bhagwati once said the Chinese were turn­ing out to be profit-seeking while Indians were rent-seeking. Amit says he doesn’t know enough about China to judge, but it rings true for India.

Oscar Lange’s pro­posal for a cen­tral price com­mit­tee was what Hayek’s ‘The Use of Knowledge in Society’ ar­gued against. Amit links it back to Bastiat’s essay on how Paris gets fed with­out any cen­tral com­mit­tee.
Adam Ferguson’s phrase ‘the prod­uct of human ac­tion but not human design’, and Adam Smith’s ‘man of system’ who treats so­ci­ety like a chess­board.

The watch­maker ar­gu­ment against nat­u­ral se­lec­tion, an­swered by Dawkins’ The Blind Watchmaker. Ajay notes that the eye is more won­der­ful than any wrist­watch found on a beach, yet has no de­signer. Amit also nods to Dennett and Pinker.
